questions.question: What are Ruby's naming conventions?
questions.title: Ruby Naming Conventions
questions.direct_answer: Ruby conventions: variables and methods are snake_case (user_name, full_name); classes and modules are CamelCase (class User; class AdminUser); constants are SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (MAX_RETRIES, VERSION); files are snake_case matching the class (user.rb holds class User; admin_user.rb holds AdminUser). Methods that return a boolean end with ? (empty?, valid?) and methods that mutate end with ! (sort!, save!). The convention is strong in Ruby: everyone follows it, so code reads predictably. RuboCop enforces it. Naming matters: a name like `each_address` reads as English, and the ?/! suffixes tell the reader what the method does at a glance.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know snake_case for vars/methods, CamelCase for classes, SCREAMING for constants, and ?/! suffixes for booleans/mutators.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using camelCase for methods (Java style) or sprinkling ! on every method (it means mutate/danger, not emphasis).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: snake_case (vars/methods), CamelCase (classes), SCREAMING_SNAKE (constants), ? for booleans, ! for mutators. Files match the class. RuboCop enforces it.

sections.title: snake_case, CamelCase, and Suffixes
sections.content: Ruby conventions: variables and methods are snake_case (user_name, full_name); classes and modules are CamelCase (class User; class AdminUser); constants are SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (MAX_RETRIES, VERSION); files are snake_case matching the class (user.rb holds class User, admin_user.rb holds AdminUser). Methods that return a boolean end with a question mark (empty?, valid?) and methods that mutate end with a bang (sort!, save!). The convention is strong in Ruby: everyone follows it, so code reads predictably, and RuboCop enforces it. Naming matters: a name like each_address reads as English, and the question and bang suffixes tell the reader what the method does at a glance.

sections.title: Conventions at a Glance
sections.content:
snake_case, CamelCase, SCREAMING, ?, ! — each with a meaning.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  V[vars/methods: snake_case] --> C[classes: CamelCase]
  C --> K[constants: SCREAMING_SNAKE]
  K --> Q[booleans: ?]
  Q --> M[mutators: !]
```

sections.title: Naming conventions
sections.content:
```ruby
# Variables and methods: snake_case
user_name = 'ada'
def full_name(first, last); "#{first} #{last}"; end

# Classes and modules: CamelCase
class AdminUser; end
module AuthHelper; end

# Constants: SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE
MAX_RETRIES = 3
VERSION = '1.0.0'

# Files: snake_case matching the class
#   app/models/admin_user.rb  -> class AdminUser
#   app/models/user.rb        -> class User

# Boolean methods end with ?
user.valid?       # returns true/false
arr.empty?

# Mutating methods end with ! (danger/mutate)
arr.sort         # new sorted array (original unchanged)
arr.sort!        # sorts IN PLACE (original changed)
user.save        # returns true/false
user.save!       # raises on failure
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using camelCase for methods (Java style) — Ruby uses snake_case.
Sprinkling ! on every method — it means mutate/danger, not emphasis.
Naming a boolean method without ? (valid, not valid?) — loses the signal.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Variables and methods are snake_case (user_name, full_name).
Classes and modules are CamelCase (class AdminUser).
Files are snake_case matching the class (admin_user.rb holds AdminUser).
Boolean methods end with ? (valid?); mutating methods end with ! (sort!).

Methods that return a boolean end with a question mark (empty?, valid?) and methods that mutate end with a bang (sort!, save!). The convention is strong in Ruby: everyone follows it, so code reads predictably, and RuboCop enforces it. Naming matters: a name like each_address reads as English, and the question and bang suffixes tell the reader what the method does at a glance. A common mistake is using camelCase for methods, which is Java style when Ruby uses snake_case, and sprinkling bang on every method, when it means mutate or danger, not emphasis.
